title: Shuttle Notice Editing
description: Make sentences concise and choose transitions that match the exact logic.
subject: rla
author: Chee Skool
reviewNotes: Reviewed for one-best-answer grammar logic, contextual editing, close distractors, and specific feedback.

questions.prompt: Choose the most concise revision: “At this point in time, the shuttle currently leaves at 8:30 p.m.”

options.text: At this point in time, the shuttle currently leaves at 8:30 p.m.
options.whyWrong: 'At this point in time' and 'currently' repeat the same idea.

options.text: The shuttle, at this current point in time, leaves at 8:30 p.m.
options.whyWrong: This preserves the redundant wording and adds interruption.

options.text: The shuttle currently leaves at 8:30 p.m.
Currently at this time now, the shuttle leaves at 8:30 p.m.
options.whyWrong: 'Currently,' 'at this time,' and 'now' repeat one another.

explanation.whyCorrect: The revision keeps the needed timing information and removes repeated phrases.
explanation.quickTip: Cut words that duplicate meaning, not words that carry a condition or fact.

questions.prompt: The 8:00 shuttle was often overcrowded; {{blank}}, the office added an 8:15 departure.

options.text: therefore
however
options.whyWrong: 'However' signals contrast, but the new departure is a response to the overcrowding.

options.text: for example
options.whyWrong: The added departure is a result, not an example of overcrowding.

options.text: meanwhile
options.whyWrong: 'Meanwhile' signals simultaneous timing rather than cause and result.

explanation.whyCorrect: 'Therefore' correctly shows that the added departure resulted from overcrowding.
explanation.quickTip: Name the relationship before choosing the transition.

questions.prompt: Choose the clearest concise revision: “Students who are in possession of bicycles should use the exterior rack.”

options.text: Students who are in possession of bicycles should use the exterior rack.
options.whyWrong: 'Who are in possession of' is unnecessarily wordy.

options.text: Bicycle-possessing students, in terms of the exterior rack, should utilize it.
options.whyWrong: The sentence replaces simple wording with inflated and unclear language.

options.text: Students, being those having bikes, should make usage of the exterior rack.
options.whyWrong: This is wordier and less natural than the original.

options.text: Students with bicycles should use the exterior rack.

explanation.whyCorrect: 'Students with bicycles' states the same condition more directly.
explanation.quickTip: Prefer the shortest wording that preserves the exact meaning.

questions.prompt: The shuttle still serves the science building. {{blank}}, the library stop has moved one block east.

options.text: For example
options.whyWrong: The library move is not an example of continuing science-building service.

options.text: However
Therefore
options.whyWrong: The library stop did not move because the science-building service continues.

options.text: Similarly
options.whyWrong: The two facts are not similar; the second contrasts with the first by describing a change.

explanation.whyCorrect: 'However' correctly signals that one part of the route remains the same while another has changed.
explanation.quickTip: Use contrast transitions when the second statement limits or differs from the first.

questions.prompt: Choose the best revision: “The reason the route changed is because road work blocks the usual turn.”

options.text: The reason the route changed is because road work blocks the usual turn.
options.whyWrong: 'The reason ... is because' redundantly expresses cause twice.

options.text: The causal reason why the route changed is due to road work that blocks the usual turn.
options.whyWrong: 'Causal reason,' 'why,' and 'due to' make the sentence unnecessarily heavy.

options.text: The route changed because road work blocks the usual turn.
Road work is the reason because of which the route changed due to the blocked turn.
options.whyWrong: This is wordy and awkward.

explanation.whyCorrect: The revision directly states the cause without repeating the cause relationship.
explanation.quickTip: When because already gives the reason, you usually do not need 'the reason is because'.

questions.prompt: Riders can view live bus locations in the app. {{blank}}, they can sign up for delay alerts.

options.text: Nevertheless
options.whyWrong: 'Nevertheless' signals unexpected contrast, but the second sentence adds another service.

options.text: As a result
options.whyWrong: Signing up for alerts is not presented as a result of viewing locations.

options.text: Instead
options.whyWrong: The two options are both available; one does not replace the other.

options.text: In addition

explanation.whyCorrect: 'In addition' correctly introduces another available service.
explanation.quickTip: For another point with the same direction, use an addition transition rather than a cause or contrast word.

options.text: The office decided to extend service by thirty minutes.
The office made a decision to extend service by thirty minutes.
options.whyWrong: 'Made a decision to' can be replaced by the direct verb 'decided to'.

options.text: The office came to a decision in regard to extending service by thirty minutes.
options.whyWrong: This adds several unnecessary phrases.

options.text: A decision was made by the office for the purpose of extending service by thirty minutes.
options.whyWrong: The passive and purpose phrase make the sentence longer without adding meaning.

explanation.whyCorrect: The direct verb 'decided' expresses the same idea more efficiently.
explanation.quickTip: Look for noun-heavy phrases that can become a direct verb.

questions.prompt: The route change begins Monday. {{blank}}, riders should check the updated map before their first trip.

options.text: For instance
options.whyWrong: Checking the map is a recommended result of the change, not an example of Monday.

options.text: Consequently
In contrast
options.whyWrong: The advice does not contrast with the route change.

options.text: Likewise
options.whyWrong: The second statement is not a parallel example of the first.

explanation.whyCorrect: 'Consequently' correctly introduces an action riders should take because the route is changing.
explanation.quickTip: Result transitions should follow a fact that creates the need for the next action.

curriculum.learningObjective: Make sentences concise and choose transitions that match the exact logic.
